The closest point has x equals 13 halves.

stem: Find all the antiderivatives of f(x) = 6x⁴ + 5x² − 5.
title: Antiderivatives of a polynomial
steps: To undo the Power Rule, raise the exponent by 1 and divide by the new exponent.
Add C, since any constant has derivative 0.

stem: Find all the antiderivatives of f(x) = 2x − cos x.
title: Basic antiderivatives
steps: ∫2x dx = x²;  ∫cos x dx = sin x
Think backward: what has derivative 2 x? x squared. What has derivative cosine x? sine x.
So the antiderivatives are x squared minus sine x plus C.
others: eˣ → eˣ;  1/x → ln x;  1/√(1 − x²) → sin⁻¹ x;  1/(1 + x²) → tan⁻¹ x
Other ones to know. You can always check by differentiating.

stem: Solve dy/dx = 4x + 4 with y(1) = 7. Find y(−2).
title: An initial value problem
steps: Find all antiderivatives of 4 x plus 4.
Use the given point to find C.

stem: An object moves along a line with acceleration a(t) = −6t, initial velocity v(0) = 5, and initial position s(0) = 7. Find s(3).
title: Position from acceleration
steps: Antidifferentiate the acceleration to get velocity. Use v of 0 to find the constant.

stem: Approximate the area under the graph of f(x) = 3x + 4 from x = 2 to x = 4 using 4 subintervals of equal width and the right endpoints of the subintervals.
title: Approximate area with a Riemann sum
steps: The width of each rectangle is the length of the interval over the number of rectangles.
Right endpoints start one width in from the left end. Left endpoints would start at 2.
Find the height of each rectangle: f at each sample point.
Add the heights and multiply by the width.

stem: Find the exact area under the graph of f(x) = 2x + 1 from x = 3 to x = 7. (The region is a trapezoid.)
title: Exact area from geometry
steps: The region under a line is a trapezoid. Its parallel sides are the heights at the ends.
Trapezoid area: one half times the sum of the parallel sides times the width.

stem:
f is continuous, with values shown.
x:  0   3   4   6   10
f(x):  10   9   11   1   6
Use a left Riemann sum with the four subintervals shown to approximate ∫₀¹⁰ f(x) dx.
title: A Riemann sum from a table
steps: The subintervals aren't equal, so find each width: 0 to 3, 3 to 4, 4 to 6, 6 to 10.
A left sum uses the value at the left end of each subinterval.
Multiply each width by its height and add.

stem: Use geometry to evaluate ∫₋₂² √(4 − x²) dx.
title: An integral as part of a circle
steps: y = √(4 − x²) → upper half of a circle, radius 2
Recognize the graph: the top half of a circle centered at the origin.
From negative 2 to 2 is the whole half-disk: one half pi r squared.

stem: Use geometry (net signed area) to evaluate ∫₁³ (2x + 2) dx.
title: An integral as signed area under a line
steps: y = 2x + 2: heights 4 at x = 1 and 8 at x = 3
The graph is a line, so the region is a trapezoid.
Area above the axis counts as positive. If part were below, it would count as negative.

stem: Which definite integral equals the limit as n → ∞ of  ∑ (from i = 1 to n) (3 + 3i/n)³ · (3/n)?
title: A Riemann sum limit as an integral
steps: The factor 3 over n is delta x, so the interval is 3 wide.
The sample point starts at 3, so a is 3 and b is 6.
The expression being cubed is x, so the function is x cubed.

stem: Evaluate ∫₋₂⁰ (6x² − 2x − 1) dx.
title: The Fundamental Theorem of Calculus
steps: Find an antiderivative of 6 x squared minus 2 x minus 1.
Evaluate at the top limit minus the bottom limit.

stem: Evaluate ∫ from 0 to 1/2 of 1/√(1 − x²) dx.
title: An integral with an inverse trig antiderivative
steps: The antiderivative of 1 over the square root of 1 minus x squared is arcsine x.
Evaluate: arcsine of one half is pi over 6.

stem: F(x) = ∫ from 2 to x of √(t² + 36) dt. Find F′(8).
title: The derivative of an integral (FTC Part 1)
steps: Part 1 of the Fundamental Theorem: the derivative of the integral from a constant to x of f of t is f of x.

stem: F(x) = ∫ from 1 to x² of (t³ + 1) dt. Find F′(1).
title: FTC Part 1 with the Chain Rule
steps: When the upper limit is x squared, plug it in and multiply by its derivative, 2 x.
So F prime is x to the 6th plus 1, times 2 x.

stem: Water flows into a tank at r(t) = 4t + 9 liters per minute. At t = 0 the tank holds 100 liters. How much water is in the tank at t = 6 minutes?
title: Accumulation: amount from a rate
steps: The amount now is the starting amount plus the integral of the rate.

stem:
∫₀¹ f(x) dx = −6,  ∫₁² f(x) dx = 7,  ∫₀¹ g(x) dx = −3.
Find ∫₀² f(x) dx.
title: Properties of definite integrals
steps: So from 0 to 2 is negative 6 plus 7, which is 1.
Also: switching the limits changes the sign, constants come out front, and sums split apart.

stem: Find the average value of f(x) = −3x² + 5 on the interval [0, 3].
title: Average value of a function
steps: The average value is the integral divided by the length of the interval.

stem: Evaluate ∫₀⁵ |x − 2| dx.
title: Integral of an absolute value
steps: |x − 2| is a V with its point at x = 2
Split the integral where the inside is 0.
The graph forms two triangles above the axis. Find each area.

stem: An object moves along a line with velocity v(t) = t − 4 m/s. Find the displacement (net change in position) from t = 0 to t = 8.
title: Displacement from velocity
steps: Displacement is the integral of velocity.
The object ends where it started.
Total distance uses the absolute value: the object goes back 8 meters and forward 8.

stem: Find ∫ xe^(x²) dx.
title: Integration by substitution
steps: u = x², du = 2x dx → x dx = (1/2) du
Choose u as the inside function. Its derivative, 2 x, appears in the integral.
Rewrite everything in u and integrate.
Put x back in. Check by differentiating.

stem: Evaluate ∫₀² x(x² + 3)³ dx.
title: Substitution in a definite integral
steps: u = x² + 3, du = 2x dx;  x = 0 → u = 3, x = 2 → u = 7
Substitute and change the limits to u values.
Evaluate: 7 to the 4th is 2401, and 3 to the 4th is 81.

stem: f is odd and ∫₀³ f(x) dx = 5. Find ∫₋₃³ f(x) dx.
title: Integral of an odd function
steps: odd: f(−x) = −f(x) → symmetric about the origin
An odd function's left half is the opposite of its right half.
The two halves cancel, so the integral is 0.

stem: f is even and ∫₀³ f(x) dx = 2. Find ∫₋₃³ f(x) dx.
title: Integral of an even function
steps: An even function's two halves are mirror images.
So the whole integral is twice the right half.

stem: Find ∫ xe^(3x) dx.
title: Integration by parts
steps: Integration by parts undoes the Product Rule.
u = x → du = dx;  dv = e^(3x) dx → v = (1/3)e^(3x)
Choose u to be the part that gets simpler when you differentiate: here, x.
Integrate what's left. Check by differentiating.

stem: Find ∫ ln x dx.
title: Integration by parts: ∫ ln x dx
steps: u = ln x → du = (1/x) dx;  dv = dx → v = x
The trick: let dv be just dx.
x ln x − ∫ x · (1/x) dx = x ln x − ∫ 1 dx
Plug into u v minus the integral of v du.

stem: Evaluate ∫₀¹ xeˣ dx.
title: Integration by parts with limits
steps: u = x, dv = eˣ dx → ∫ xeˣ dx = xeˣ − eˣ
First find the antiderivative by parts.

stem: To find ∫ xe^(3x) dx by parts, which choice of u and dv works best?
title: Choosing u and dv
steps: u: the part that gets simpler when differentiated
Choose u so that du is simpler. The usual order is logarithms and inverse trig first, then powers of x, then trig and exponentials.
∫ xe^(3x) dx: u = x, dv = e^(3x) dx
Here x gets simpler, and e to the 3 x is easy to integrate.

stem: Find ∫ sin(3x)cos(2x) dx.
title: Integrate a product of sines and cosines with different angles
steps: Use the product-to-sum formula: sine A cosine B is one half of sine of A plus B plus sine of A minus B.

stem: Find ∫ sin x cos² x dx.
title: Trigonometric integrals
steps: ∫ sin x cos² x dx: u = cos x, du = −sin x dx
With an odd power of sine or cosine, save one factor for du and substitute.
Put cosine back. Even powers need the power-reducing identities instead, like sine squared equals 1 minus cosine 2 x, over 2.

stem: Evaluate ∫₀^π sin² x dx.
title: A definite trigonometric integral
steps: An even power: use the power-reducing identity.
Sine of 2 pi and sine of 0 are both 0.

stem: Which substitution should be used to find an integral containing √(x² − 25)?
title: Choosing a trigonometric substitution
steps: √(a² − x²) → x = a sin θ;  √(x² + a²) → x = a tan θ;  √(x² − a²) → x = a sec θ
Each form matches a Pythagorean identity.
x squared minus a number: use secant. Then x squared minus 25 becomes 25 tangent squared.

stem: Find ∫ 1/√(4 − x²) dx.
title: Trig substitution: 1/√(a² − x²)
steps: x = 2 sin θ, dx = 2 cos θ dθ;  √(4 − x²) = 2 cos θ
∫ (2 cos θ)/(2 cos θ) dθ = ∫ dθ = θ

stem: Find ∫ 1/(x² + 16) dx.
title: Trig substitution: 1/(x² + a²)
steps: x = 4 tan θ, dx = 4 sec² θ dθ;  x² + 16 = 16 sec² θ
It simplifies to one fourth theta.

stem: Find ∫ 1/√(x² + 25) dx.
title: Trig substitution: 1/√(x² + a²)
steps: x = 5 tan θ → ∫ sec θ dθ
Substitute with tangent. The integral becomes secant theta.
Use the known antiderivative of secant.
tan θ = x/5, sec θ = √(x² + 25)/5 → ln|x + √(x² + 25)| + C
Go back to x with a triangle. The 5s combine into the constant C.

stem: Evaluate ∫ from 0 to 3 of dx/(x² + 9).
title: A definite integral with trig substitution

stem: Find ∫ dx/(x² + 6x + 18).
title: Complete the square
steps: Complete the square in the denominator.

stem: Find ∫ (x² − 3x + 5)/(x − 1) dx.
title: Long division before integrating
steps: The top's degree isn't smaller, so divide first.
Integrate each piece. The remainder piece gives a natural log.

stem: Evaluate ∫ from 3 to 4 of dx/(x² − 6x + 10).
title: Complete the square with limits
steps: Change the limits: x from 3 to 4 means u from 0 to 1.

title: Partial fraction decomposition
steps: Multiply both sides by the denominator.
Plug in x equals negative 3 to make the B term vanish.
Plug in negative 2 to find B.

title: Integrate with partial fractions
steps: Split into partial fractions: multiply through and plug in negative 1 and negative 2.
Each piece integrates to a natural log.

stem: Evaluate ∫ from 3 to 6 of dx/(x(x + 2)).
title: Partial fractions with limits
steps: Evaluate: 3 fourths divided by 3 fifths is 5 fourths.

stem: Approximate ∫ from 0 to 4 of x² + 1 dx with a trapezoidal sum using n = 4 subintervals of equal width.
title: The trapezoidal rule
steps: Find the width and the function values at each point.
The inside values count twice, because each is shared by two trapezoids.
Add and multiply by one half.

stem:
f is continuous, with values shown.
x:  1   3   4   7   9
f(x):  10   9   11   1   6
Use a trapezoidal sum with the four subintervals shown to approximate ∫₁⁹ f(x) dx.
title: A trapezoidal sum from a table
steps: trapezoid = width × (average of the two heights)
The widths aren't equal, so find each trapezoid separately.

stem: Approximate ∫ from 0 to 4 of x² + 1 dx with Simpson’s Rule using n = 4.
title: Simpson's Rule
steps: n is 4, so the width is 1. Find each function value.

stem: f is increasing and its graph is concave up on [a, b]. Is a trapezoidal sum for ∫ from a to b of f(x) dx an overestimate or an underestimate?
title: Trapezoidal sums: over or under?
steps: concave up → trapezoids lie above the curve
The tops of the trapezoids are straight lines connecting points on the graph. If the graph is concave up, those lines are above it.
So the trapezoidal sum is an overestimate. Concave down would give an underestimate.

stem: f is decreasing and its graph is concave down on [a, b]. Is a left Riemann sum for ∫ from a to b of f(x) dx an overestimate or an underestimate?
title: Riemann sums: over or under?
steps: decreasing → left endpoints are the highest
Left and right sums depend on increasing or decreasing, not concavity.
left sum on a decreasing function → overestimate
Each rectangle uses the taller left side, so the sum is too big. For an increasing function it would be an underestimate.

stem: Determine whether ∫ from 1 to ∞ of dx/x³ converges or diverges. If it converges, find its value.
title: Improper integrals with powers
steps: From 1 to infinity, the power has to be bigger than 1. From 0 to 1, it has to be smaller than 1.
Integrate and take the limit as b goes to infinity.

stem: Determine whether ∫ from 0 to ∞ of e^(4x) dx converges or diverges. If it converges, find its value.
title: An improper integral with eᵏˣ
steps: Replace infinity with b and integrate.
e to the 4 b grows without bound, so it diverges. With a negative exponent, it would converge.

stem: Determine whether ∫ from 0 to ∞ of xe^(−x) dx converges or diverges. If it converges, find its value.
title: An improper integral with xe^(−x)
steps: As b goes to infinity, both terms go to 0. At 0, it's negative 1.

stem: Evaluate ∫ from 0 to ∞ of dx/(1 + x²).
title: Evaluating an improper integral
steps: Replace infinity with b and take a limit.

stem: Which technique should you try first to find ∫ sin³ x dx?
title: Which technique first?
steps: look at the form of the integrand
sin³ x → trig identity (odd power: save one sin x)
Powers of trig functions use identities.
others: u-sub (inside's derivative is there), parts (product like x cos x), partial fractions, trig sub (√(a² − x²)), long division

Other signals: an inside function whose derivative is present means u-substitution; a product like x cosine x means parts; a factorable denominator means partial fractions; a square root of a squared expression means trig substitution; a top degree too big means long division.

stem: f is decreasing and its graph is concave up on [a, b]. Is a midpoint sum for ∫ from a to b of f(x) dx an overestimate or an underestimate?
title: Midpoint sums: over or under?
steps: A midpoint rectangle is the same as a trapezoid tilted to match the tangent line at the midpoint.
concave up → tangent lines lie below the curve → underestimate
When the graph is concave up, the tangent lines are below it, so the midpoint sum is an underestimate. Concave down gives an overestimate: the opposite of the trapezoidal sum.

stem: State the order of the differential equation and whether it is linear or nonlinear:   y″ + sin y = 0
title: Order and linearity of a differential equation
steps: The order of a differential equation is the highest derivative in it.
Here the highest derivative is y double prime, so the order is 2.
Linear: y, y′, y″ only to the first power, times functions of x
A linear equation has y and its derivatives only to the first power, never inside another function.
Sine of y puts y inside a function, so this equation is nonlinear. Order 2, nonlinear.

stem: For which values of k is y = e^(kx) a solution of y″ − 7y′ + 10y = 0?
title: Find k so that y = e^(kx) is a solution
steps: y = e^(kx), y′ = ke^(kx), y″ = k²e^(kx)
Find the first and second derivatives of e to the k x.
Substitute them into the differential equation.
Factor out e to the k x. It is never zero, so the other factor must be zero.
Solve the quadratic: k equals 2 and k equals 5.

stem: Find the particular solution of dy/dx = eˣ + 2sin(2x) with y(0) = −1.
title: Find a particular solution
steps: Integrate both sides to get the general solution.
y(0) = e⁰ − cos 0 + C = 1 − 1 + C = C
Use the initial condition: substitute x = 0.
Set it equal to the given value, negative 1.
Put C back in to get the particular solution.

stem: Solve dy/dx = 6x − 5 with y(0) = −2. Find y(−2).
title: Use an initial condition, then evaluate
steps: Integrate to get the general solution.
Substitute the initial condition to find C.
Now evaluate at the requested x-value.

stem: Solve dy/dx = x/y with y(0) = 5 (y > 0). Find y(12).
title: Separation of variables: dy/dx = x/y
steps: Separate: put every y on the side with d y and every x on the side with d x.
Use the initial condition to find the constant.
Take the positive root, since y is positive, and evaluate.

stem: Solve dy/dx = 2xy with y(0) = 2. Find y(1).
title: Separation of variables: exponential solution
steps: Divide by y and multiply by d x to separate the variables.
Use the initial condition to find C.

stem: Solve dy/dx = y² with y(0) = 1. Find y(−1).
title: Separation of variables: dy/dx = y²
steps: Divide by y squared to separate the variables.
Integrate: the antiderivative of y to the negative 2 is negative 1 over y.

stem: A bacteria population grows at a rate proportional to its size and doubles every 8 hours. If there are 800 bacteria now, how many will there be after 24 hours?
title: Exponential growth with a doubling time
steps: Growth proportional to size means exponential growth.
Count how many doubling times fit into the elapsed time.
Each doubling time multiplies the amount by 2.

stem: A radioactive substance has a half-life of 3 years. If 200 grams are present now, how much will remain after 3 years?
title: Exponential decay with a half-life
steps: Count how many half-lives fit into the elapsed time.
Each half-life multiplies the amount by one half. 100 grams remain.

stem: A population grows according to P = P₀e^(kt) and doubles every 10 years. Find k.
title: Find k from a doubling time
steps: After 10 years the population is twice P naught. Divide out P naught.
Take the natural log of both sides.

stem: A substance decays according to A = A₀e^(kt) and has a half-life of 2 years. Find k.
title: Find k from a half-life
steps: After one half-life, half of A naught is left.
Take the natural log of both sides. The log of one half is negative log 2.
Divide by 2. For decay, k is negative.

stem: An object at 230° is placed in a room at 70°. By Newton’s Law of Cooling, the difference between its temperature and the room’s halves every 15 minutes. What is its temperature after 45 minutes?
title: Newton's Law of Cooling
steps: The difference between the object and the room decays exponentially.
The difference halves every 15 minutes, so 45 minutes is 3 halvings.

stem: The slope field shown represents solutions of which differential equation?
title: Match a slope field to its equation
steps: Check points where the slope is easy to see
Pick a few points and compare the segment there to each equation.
The segments are flat along both axes, so the right side is zero when x = 0 or y = 0.
In the first quadrant the slope is positive. In the second it is negative.
Only x y matches every check.

stem: In the slope field for dy/dx = 2x + 2y, what is the slope of the segment at the point (1, 3)?
title: Slope of a segment in a slope field
steps: The segment's slope is the value of d y d x at that point.
Substitute x = 1 and y = 3. The slope is 8.

stem: Where are the segments in the slope field for dy/dx = x² − y horizontal?
title: Where the slope field is horizontal
steps: Set the right side equal to zero.
The segments are horizontal along the parabola y = x squared.

stem: Use Euler’s Method with step size h = 0.25 to approximate y(1.5) for dy/dx = xy, y(1) = 3.
title: Euler's Method
steps: Each step adds the step size times the slope at the current point.
Start at the initial point. The slope there is 3.
Move to x = 1.25 and find the new slope.
Take the second step. That reaches x = 1.5, so y of 1.5 is about 4.92.

stem: A population grows according to dP/dt = 0.000417P(1200 − P). What is the population when it is growing most rapidly?
title: Logistic growth: fastest growth
steps: In logistic form, the carrying capacity M is the number subtracted from P.
The growth rate is largest halfway to the carrying capacity, at the inflection point.
So the population grows fastest at 600.

stem: P(t) = 100/(1 + 3e^(−0.2t)). What is the limit of P(t) as t → ∞ (the carrying capacity)?
title: Carrying capacity of a logistic function
steps: A logistic function has this shape: M over 1 plus A e to the negative k t.
As t grows, the exponential term goes to zero.
The population approaches 100, the carrying capacity.

stem: P(t) = 600/(1 + 19e^(−0.05t)). At what time t is the population growing most rapidly?
title: When a logistic population grows fastest
steps: Fastest growth is at half the carrying capacity.
Set P equal to 300 and simplify.
Isolate the exponential and take the natural log.

stem: P(t) = 500/(1 + 4e^(−0.5t)). What is the initial population P(0)?
title: Initial value of a logistic function
steps: Any number to the zero power is 1. The initial population is 100.

stem: Find the area of the region bounded by the graphs of y = x² and y = 4x − 3.
title: Area between two curves
steps: Set the curves equal to find where they cross. Those are the limits.
Test a point between them to see which graph is on top.

stem: Which integral gives the area of the region bounded by y = eˣ, y = x, x = 1, and x = 2?
title: Set up an area integral
steps: Decide which graph is on top over the whole interval.
The area integral is top minus bottom, between the given x-values.
Here the top is e to the x and the bottom is x.

stem: Find the area of the region bounded by y = x³ and y = x (both pieces).
title: Area when the curves cross more than once
steps: Find all the intersections: the curves switch places at x = 0.
[−1, 0]: x³ on top;  [0, 1]: x on top
Check which is on top on each piece.
Integrate top minus bottom on each piece. Each area is one fourth.
Add the pieces. One integral of x cubed minus x over the whole interval would wrongly give zero.

stem: Find the area of the region bounded by x = 9 − y² and the y-axis.
title: Area integrating with respect to y
steps: The curve meets the y-axis, x = 0, at y = plus or minus 3.
With respect to y, integrate right minus left. The left boundary is x = 0.

stem: Find the volume of the solid formed by revolving the region bounded by y = eˣ, the x-axis, x = 0, and x = 1 about the x-axis.
title: Disk method
steps: Each slice is a disk whose radius is the height of the region.
R(x) = eˣ → V = π∫₀¹ e^(2x) dx
The radius is e to the x. Squaring gives e to the 2 x.

stem: Find the volume of the solid formed by revolving the region bounded by y = x² and y = 4 about the x-axis.
title: Washer method
steps: Find where the curves meet to get the limits.
The outer radius goes to the farther curve, the inner radius to the nearer one.
V = π∫₋₂² (R² − r²) dx = π∫₋₂² (16 − x⁴) dx
Square each radius separately and subtract. Do not square R minus r.

stem: The region bounded by y = x², the x-axis, and x = 1 is revolved about the line y = 4. Which integral gives the volume?
title: Revolving around a horizontal line
steps: Axis y = 4 is above the region
Measure each radius from the axis, the line y = 4.
The farther boundary is the x-axis, distance 4. The nearer is the curve, distance 4 minus x squared.
Use the washer formula: pi times the integral of R squared minus r squared.

stem: The region in the first quadrant bounded by y = x³, the y-axis, and y = 8 is revolved about the y-axis. Find the volume.
title: Disks around the y-axis
steps: Revolving around the y-axis, write the radius as a function of y.
V = π∫₀⁸ (y^(1/3))² dy = π∫₀⁸ y^(2/3) dy
Disks stacked along the y-axis, from y = 0 to y = 8.
Eight to the five thirds is 32.

stem: The region bounded by y = 2x − x² and the x-axis is revolved about the y-axis. What is the radius of a typical shell?
title: Radius of a shell
steps: Shell radius = distance from the slice to the axis
A vertical slice at x, spun around the y-axis, makes a shell.
The distance from x to the y-axis is just x.

stem: The region bounded by y = 2x − x² and the x-axis is revolved about the line x = 4. Which integral gives the volume using shells?
title: Shells around a vertical line
steps: The shell method: 2 pi times radius times height.
The axis x = 4 is to the right, so the distance is 4 minus x. The height is the curve.
The region runs from x = 0 to x = 2.

stem: Use the shell method to find the volume of the solid formed by revolving the region bounded by y = 1/x, the x-axis, x = 1, and x = 4 about the y-axis.
title: Shell method
steps: Around the y-axis, the radius is x and the height is f of x.
Here the height is 1 over x, so the product is 1.

stem: Cross sections of a solid are squares, where s is the width of the base at x. Which gives the area A(x) of a cross section?
title: Square cross sections
steps: Cross section: square with side s
The side of each square is the width of the base at x.
A square with side s has area s squared.

stem: Cross sections of a solid are equilateral triangles, where s is the width of the base at x. Which gives the area A(x) of a cross section?
title: Equilateral triangle cross sections
steps: An equilateral triangle with side s has height root 3 over 2 times s.
Multiply one half base times height.

stem: Cross sections of a solid are semicircles whose diameters lie across the base, where s is the width of the base at x. Which gives the area A(x) of a cross section?
title: Semicircle cross sections
steps: The diameter is s, so the radius is s over 2.
A semicircle is half of pi r squared.

stem: Cross sections of a solid are isosceles right triangles with one leg on the base, where s is the width of the base at x. Which gives the area A(x) of a cross section?
title: Isosceles right triangle cross sections
steps: An isosceles right triangle has two equal legs, and they are the base and height.
With legs of length s, the area is one half s squared.

stem: The base of a solid is the region bounded by y = 2 − x, the x-axis, and the y-axis. Cross sections perpendicular to the x-axis are isosceles right triangles with one leg on the base. Find the volume.
title: Volume by cross sections
steps: The width of the base at x is the height of the line, 2 minus x.
Use the area formula for the cross section.
Volume is the integral of the cross-section area.
The integral of 2 minus x squared from 0 to 2 is 8 thirds.

stem: Find the arc length of the graph of y = x³/6 + 1/(2x) from x = 1 to x = 2.
title: Arc length that simplifies to a perfect square
steps: Squaring and adding 1 just flips the minus sign to a plus: a perfect square.
The square root undoes the square.

stem: Find the arc length of the graph of y = (2/3)x^(3/2) from x = 0 to x = 3.
title: Arc length of y = (2/3)x^(3/2)
steps: The derivative is root x. Squaring gives x.
Set up the arc length integral.
Integrate and evaluate. Four to the three halves is 8.

stem: Find the arc length of the graph of y = 3x − 1 from x = 1 to x = 2.
title: Arc length of a line
steps: The slope is constant, so the integrand is constant.
Integrate over an interval of length 1. It matches the distance formula.

stem: Which integral gives the length of the graph of y = 3x⁴ from x = 0 to x = 3?
title: Set up an arc length integral
steps: Start from the arc length formula.

stem: Which integrand gives the arc length of y = sin x?  (s = ∫ ____ dx over the interval)
title: Arc length integrand
steps: The arc length integrand is the square root of 1 plus the derivative squared.
The derivative of sine is cosine.

stem: A force of 10 N is required to keep a spring stretched 1 m beyond its natural length. How much work (in joules) is done in stretching it from its natural length to 1.5 m beyond its natural length?
title: Work stretching a spring
steps: Hooke's Law: use the given force and stretch to find k.
Work is the integral of force over the distance, from natural length to 1.5 meters.

stem: How much work (in joules) is done by a variable force F(x) = (30 − x) N that moves an object along a straight line from x = 0 m to x = 5 m?
title: Work done by a variable force
steps: Work by a variable force is the integral of the force.

stem: A 10-ft chain weighing 3 lb/ft hangs from the top of a building. How much work (in ft-lb) is done in pulling the entire chain to the top?
title: Work pulling up a hanging chain
steps: Piece at depth y weighs 3Δy, lifted y ft
A small piece of chain at depth y has to be lifted y feet.
Add up weight times distance for every piece.

stem: A 25-lb bucket hangs at the end of a 40-ft chain weighing 5 lb/ft from the top of a building. How much work (in ft-lb) is done in pulling the bucket and chain to the top?
title: Work lifting a bucket and chain
steps: Each piece of chain is lifted its depth y.
The bucket's weight is constant, lifted the full 40 feet.

stem: A cylindrical tank with radius 5 ft and height 10 ft is full of water (weight density 62.4 lb/ft³). How much work (in ft-lb) is required to pump all the water to a level 2 ft above the top of the tank?
title: Work pumping water out of a tank
steps: Slice at depth y: volume π(5)²Δy, weight 62.4π(25)Δy
Each thin slice of water is a disk of radius 5.
A slice at depth y rises y feet to the top, then 2 more.
Weight times distance, added over the whole depth.

stem: A curve is given by x(t) = 2t² + 2t + 1, y(t) = 3t − 4. What point is on the curve when t = −1?
title: A point on a parametric curve
steps: Substitute t = negative 1 into x of t.
Substitute the same t into y of t.

stem: Find a rectangular equation for the plane curve x(t) = 2t + 2,  y(t) = 3t + 2.
title: Eliminate the parameter
steps: Solve the x equation for t.
Substitute that expression for t into the y equation.
This rectangular equation is a line.

stem: For x(t) = −5 sin t, y(t) = 5 cos t, 0 ≤ t ≤ 2π, how is the circle traced?
title: Direction a parametric circle is traced
steps: Find the starting point at t = 0.
Find the point a quarter turn later.
(0, 5) → (−5, 0): from the top to the left
Moving from the top of the circle to the left side is counterclockwise.

stem: Find the slope of the tangent line to x(t) = t² + 2t, y(t) = t³ + 4t at t = −2.
title: Slope of a parametric curve
steps: Divide the y rate by the x rate.

stem: For x(t) = t² + 3, y(t) = t³ − 27t, at which values of t is the tangent line horizontal?
title: Horizontal tangents of a parametric curve
steps: The tangent is horizontal when y stops changing but x does not.
Set d y d t equal to zero.
Check that d x d t is not also zero there. At t = 0, d x d t is zero, which is a vertical tangent.

stem: For x(t) = t + 1, y(t) = t³, find d²y/dx² at t = 3.
title: Second derivative of a parametric curve
steps: First find d y d x.
Differentiate d y d x with respect to t, then divide by d x d t again.

stem: Find the length of the curve x = 3t, y = 4t, 0 ≤ t ≤ 2.
title: Length of a parametric curve
steps: Arc length adds up the speed over time.

stem: Which integral gives the length of the curve x(t) = 3t³, y(t) = t⁴, 0 ≤ t ≤ 3?
title: Set up a parametric arc length integral

stem: Convert the polar point (6, 5π/3) to rectangular coordinates.
title: Polar to rectangular coordinates
steps: x = r cos θ,  y = r sin θ
Five pi over 3 is in Quadrant 4, where cosine is positive.
Sine is negative there. The point is 3, negative 3 root 3.

stem: What kind of graph is r = 4 + 4 sin θ?
title: Limaçons and cardioids
steps: r = a + b sin θ: compare a and b
For r = a plus b sine or cosine, compare the two numbers.
a = b: cardioid;  a < b: inner loop;  a > b: no loop
Equal gives a cardioid. a smaller gives an inner loop. a larger gives a limaçon with no loop.
Here they are equal, so it is a cardioid.

stem: What kind of graph is r² = 2 cos(2θ)?
title: Lemniscates
steps: r² = a² cos(2θ) or r² = a² sin(2θ)
r squared equals a constant times cosine or sine of 2 theta.
That form is a lemniscate, a figure-eight.

stem: How many petals does the rose r = 3 cos(4θ) have?
title: Petals of a rose curve
steps: r = a cos(nθ) or a sin(nθ)
A rose curve has n inside the trig function.
n odd → n petals;  n even → 2n petals
Odd n gives n petals. Even n gives twice as many.
Four is even, so there are 8 petals.

stem: Find the slope of the tangent line to the polar curve r = 2 sin θ at θ = π/6.
title: Slope of a polar curve
steps: dy/dx = (r′ sin θ + r cos θ)/(r′ cos θ − r sin θ)
Use x = r cos theta and y = r sine theta, and differentiate with respect to theta.
Find r and r prime at theta = pi over 6.

stem: Find the arc length of the polar curve r = e^θ from θ = 0 to θ = 1.
title: Arc length of a polar curve
steps: For r = e to the theta, r prime is also e to the theta.
The square root is root 2 e to the theta. Integrate from 0 to 1.

stem: Find the area enclosed by the circle r = 3 cos θ.
title: Area enclosed by a polar circle
steps: Polar area is one half the integral of r squared.
r = 3 cos θ traces the circle once for 0 ≤ θ ≤ π
This circle is traced once as theta goes from 0 to pi.
Evaluate. It matches pi r squared with radius 3 halves.

stem: Find the area of one petal of the rose r = 2 cos(2θ).
title: Area of one petal of a rose
steps: One petal runs between the angles where r is zero.
Use one half the integral of r squared over one petal.
The integral of cosine squared over that interval is pi over 4.

stem: Find the area of the region bounded by r = 4θ, θ = 0, and θ = π/2.
title: Area swept by a polar curve
steps: Polar area: one half the integral of r squared.

stem: Where do the graphs of r = 4 cos θ and r = 2 intersect?
title: Where two polar curves intersect
steps: Set the two r expressions equal.
Setting the equations equal can miss the pole, where the curves can pass at different angles.

stem: Which integral gives the area of the region inside r = 4 cos θ and outside r = 2?
title: Area between two polar curves
steps: The curves meet at plus and minus pi over 3: those are the limits.
Outer radius squared minus inner radius squared. Square each separately.
(1/2)∫ from −π/3 to π/3 of (16cos² θ − 4) dθ
Here R is 4 cosine theta and r is 2.

stem: Find the domain of r(t) = ⟨√(5 − t), ln(t + 4)⟩.
title: Domain of a vector-valued function
steps: A square root needs a nonnegative input.
A logarithm needs a positive input.
The domain is where both components are defined.

stem: Find the limit of r(t) = ⟨(t² − 16)/(t − 4), t² + 2⟩ as t → 4.
title: Limit of a vector-valued function
steps: Take the limit of each component
A vector limit works component by component.

stem: Find the arc length of r(t) = ⟨eᵗ cos t, eᵗ sin t⟩ from t = 0 to t = 1.
title: Arc length of a vector-valued function
steps: Length is the integral of speed.
r′ = ⟨eᵗ(cos t − sin t), eᵗ(sin t + cos t)⟩ → ‖r′‖ = √2 eᵗ
Use the Product Rule on each component. The squares add to 2 e to the 2 t.

stem: A particle moves along the curve r(t) = ⟨t³ + 2t, t² + 3t⟩. Find its acceleration at t = 0.
title: Velocity and acceleration vectors
steps: Velocity is the derivative of position.
Acceleration is the derivative of velocity.

stem: A particle moves along r(t) = ⟨4t², 6t⟩. Find its speed at t = 1.
title: Speed of a particle
steps: Differentiate to get velocity, then evaluate.
Speed is the magnitude of the velocity vector.

stem: An object of mass 10 kg moves along r(t) = ⟨5 cos(3t), 5 sin(3t)⟩ (meters, seconds). Find the magnitude of the force acting on it, in newtons.
title: Force on an object moving in a circle
steps: Differentiate twice. Each derivative brings out a factor of 3.
The magnitude is the radius times 3 squared.
Newton's Second Law: force equals mass times acceleration.

stem: Find the integral from 0 to 3 of ⟨3t, t²⟩ dt.
title: Definite integral of a vector-valued function
Position from velocity and an initial point
steps: Integrate each component, with its own constant.
Use the initial position to find the constants.

stem: A projectile is fired from ground level at 96 ft/s at an angle of 60° to the horizontal (g = 32 ft/s²). What is its range (in feet)?
title: Range of a projectile
steps: Horizontal motion is constant speed. Vertical motion has gravity.
Set the height to zero to find when it lands.
Substitute that time into x, which gives the range formula.
